label: prop:transport
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $J_t(x)$ be the positive Riemannian Jacobian of $\Phi_t$. Change of variables gives
\[
\mu_\theta(\Phi_t(D))
=\int_D \rho_\theta(\Phi_t(x))J_t(x)\,dV_g(x).
\]
Along the flow, $\dot J_t=(\operatorname{div}_g f)\circ\Phi_t\,J_t$. Since $D$ has compact closure, differentiation under the integral sign is justified on every bounded time interval on which the image remains in a compact flow tube. Hence
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\mu_\theta(\Phi_t(D))
=\int_D\big(\mathcal{L}_f\rho_\theta+\rho_\theta\operatorname{div}_gf\big)(\Phi_t(x))J_t(x)\,dV_g(x),
\]
and changing variables back yields \eqref{eq:transport}. Finally,
$\mathcal{L}_f\rho_\theta=\rho_\theta\theta^\top\mathcal{L}_f\psi$, and the last equality in \eqref{eq:Dtheta} is the product rule for divergence.
head: environment

label: rem:power
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:power}
For $p=1$, let $w>0$ be $C^1$ and choose $\psi=\ln w$, $\theta=\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. Then
\[
\rho_\alpha=w^\alpha,\qquad
D_\alpha f=\operatorname{div}_gf+\alpha\mathcal{L}_f\ln w
=w^{-\alpha}\operatorname{div}_g(w^\alpha f).
\]
Thus the power-weighted phase volume is a one-parameter subfamily of the density-divergence construction.
head: environment

label: th:design
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each fixed $x\in K$, the function $-a(x)-\theta^\top b(x)$ is affine in $\theta$. The pointwise minimum of affine functions is concave, proving the first statement in item 1. For any $\theta_1,\theta_2$,
\[
-a(x)-\theta_1^\top b(x)
\ge -a(x)-\theta_2^\top b(x)-B_K\|\theta_1-\theta_2\|_2.
\]
Taking the minimum over $x$ and then interchanging $\theta_1,\theta_2$ gives \eqref{eq:lipschitz}. Hence $q_K$ is continuous.

Equation \eqref{eq:halfspaces} follows directly from the pointwise inequalities. It is an intersection of the compact convex set $\Theta$ with closed half-spaces, so it is compact and convex. Finally, continuity of $q_K$ and compactness of $\Theta$ imply attainment of \eqref{eq:qstar}. The hypograph formulation of the max-min problem is exactly \eqref{eq:sip}. All constraints are affine in $(\theta,\lambda)$. Finally, $\theta\mapsto\operatorname{osc}_K(\theta^\top\psi)$ is convex because it is the sum of the convex support function $\max_K\theta^\top\psi$ and the convex function $\max_K(-\theta^\top\psi)$. Therefore \eqref{eq:Theta-kappa} is a closed convex subset of the compact set $\Theta$.
head: environment

label: prop:active
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $\bar\theta$ maximizes $q_K$. Because $K$ is compact and the affine integrand in \eqref{eq:q} is jointly continuous in $(x,\theta)$, Danskin's theorem for a pointwise minimum gives
\[
\partial^+q_K(\bar\theta)
=\operatorname{co}\{-b(x):x\in X(\bar\theta)\},
\]
see the original max--min result in \cite{Danskin66}. The first-order condition for maximizing a finite concave function over a closed convex set is
$\partial^+q_K(\bar\theta)\cap N_{\Theta}(\bar\theta)\ne\varnothing$, see, e.g., \cite{BoydVandenberghe04}. Thus some convex combination of active supergradients belongs to the normal cone. By Carath\'eodory's theorem, at most $p+1$ active points are required, which proves \eqref{eq:normal-cert}.

Conversely, suppose active points and weights satisfy \eqref{eq:normal-cert}, and set
\[
g:=-\sum_{i=1}^m\nu_i b(x_i)\in N_{\Theta}(\bar\theta).
\]
For every $\theta\in\Theta$, the definition of $q_K$ and activity of the $x_i$ give
\begin{align*}
q_K(\theta)
&\le \sum_{i=1}^m\nu_i[-a(x_i)-\theta^\top b(x_i)]\\
&=q_K(\bar\theta)+g^\top(\theta-\bar\theta)
\le q_K(\bar\theta),
\end{align*}
where the last inequality is the normal-cone condition. Hence $\bar\theta$ is a global maximizer. If $\bar\theta$ is interior to $\Theta$, then $N_{\Theta}(\bar\theta)=\{0\}$, so \eqref{eq:normal-cert} reduces to \eqref{eq:balance}. 
The converse just proved shows that this balance condition is also sufficient.
head: environment

label: prop:minimax
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Because the image of $K$ under $x\mapsto(a(x),b(x))$ is compact, its convex hull $\mathcal C_K$ is compact in the finite-dimensional space $\mathbb{R}^{p+1}$. For
\[
F(\theta,A,B):=-A-\theta^\top B,
\]
the minimum over the generating set equals the minimum over its convex hull, since $F$ is affine in $(A,B)$. Hence
\[
q_K^*=\max_{\theta\in\Theta}\min_{(A,B)\in\mathcal C_K}F(\theta,A,B).
\]
Both feasible sets are compact and convex, and $F$ is continuous and affine in each argument. Sion's minimax theorem \cite{Sion58} therefore yields
\[
q_K^*=\min_{(A,B)\in\mathcal C_K}\max_{\theta\in\Theta}F(\theta,A,B),
\]
which is \eqref{eq:minimax-dual}. Attainment follows from compactness. Carath\'eodory's theorem in $\mathbb{R}^{p+1}$ gives the representation \eqref{eq:finite-dual-support} with at most $p+2$ points.

For the finite-support statement, choose a dual optimizer $(A^*,B^*)$ and the prescribed primal optimizer $\theta^*$. The minimax equality implies
$F(\theta^*,A^*,B^*)=q_K^*$. By Carath\'eodory, represent $(A^*,B^*)$ by at most $p+2$ points and discard zero coefficients. Since
$-a(x)-{\theta^*}^\top b(x)\ge q_K^*$ for every $x\in K$, while their positive weighted average equals $q_K^*$, every supporting point must satisfy equality and hence belongs to $X(\theta^*)$.
head: environment

label: prop:grid
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any $x\in K$, choose $z\in G_\varepsilon$ with $d(x,z)\le\varepsilon$. Cauchy--Schwarz and the Lipschitz assumptions give
\[
-a(x)-\theta^\top b(x)
\ge-a(z)-\theta^\top b(z)
-(L_a+\|\theta\|_2L_b)\varepsilon.
\]
Taking the minimum over $x$ proves \eqref{eq:grid-bound}, \eqref{eq:grid-cert} then implies the continuum inequality.
head: environment

label: rem:computation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:computation}
For design over compact $\Theta$, let $R_\Theta:=\max_{\theta\in\Theta}\|\theta\|_2$. Replacing $\|\theta\|_2$ in \eqref{eq:grid-cert} by $R_\Theta$ gives the uniform sufficient constraints
\[
a(z)+\theta^\top b(z)
\le-\lambda-(L_a+R_\Theta L_b)\varepsilon,
\qquad z\in G_\varepsilon.
\]
These constraints are affine in $(\theta,\lambda)$. Hence, for polyhedral $\Theta$, the sampled certified max-margin problem is a linear program. Retaining the sharper parameter-dependent norm in \eqref{eq:grid-cert} instead gives a convex norm-constrained problem. Proposition~\ref{prop:grid} supplies the continuum guarantee, and the grid may be refined where the sampled residual is smallest.
head: environment

label: rem:constraint
title: Remark
head: environment

label: cor:alpha
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
At a point where $b(x)>0$, the inequality $a(x)+\alpha b(x)\le-\lambda$ is equivalent to
$\alpha\le(-\lambda-a(x))/b(x)$; taking all such points gives $\alpha\le U_\lambda$. At a point where $b(x)<0$, it is equivalent to the lower bound $\alpha\ge(-\lambda-a(x))/b(x)$, hence $\alpha\ge L_\lambda$. Points with $b(x)=0$ impose exactly \eqref{eq:zero-compat}. Therefore the finite feasible exponents are precisely \eqref{eq:alpha-interval}. Such a real number exists exactly under \eqref{eq:interval-nonempty}.
head: environment

label: th:contraction
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Positive invariance gives $\Phi_t(D)\subseteq K$. Proposition~\ref{prop:transport} and \eqref{eq:Dnegative} imply
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\mu_\theta(\Phi_t(D))
\le-\lambda\mu_\theta(\Phi_t(D)).
\]
Gronwall's inequality yields \eqref{eq:exp-contract}.
head: environment

label: rem:nullsets
title: Remark
head: environment

label: prop:invariant
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume, to the contrary, that $\mu_\theta(A)>0$. By \eqref{eq:equivmeas} on the compact set $A$, $\operatorname{vol}_g(A)>0$. Since $A$ is Jordan measurable, its boundary has zero volume. If $\operatorname{int}A$ were empty, compactness would imply $A=\partial A$ and hence $\operatorname{vol}_g(A)=0$, a contradiction. Thus $\operatorname{int}A\ne\varnothing$.

Invariance and Proposition~\ref{prop:transport}, applied to the compact measurable set $A$, give at $t=0$
\[
0=\int_A D_\theta f\,\rho_\theta\,dV_g.
\]
The integrand is nonpositive, so $D_\theta f=0$ almost everywhere on $A$. By continuity, it must vanish everywhere on the open set $\operatorname{int}A$: otherwise a point with a negative value would have a neighborhood of positive volume on which the integrand is strictly negative. But density of $\{D_\theta f<0\}$ forces this set to intersect $\operatorname{int}A$, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: th:discrete
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Equation \eqref{eq:change-map} is the change-of-variables formula. Under \eqref{eq:disc-cond}, $J_\theta P\le e^{-\gamma}$, hence
$\mu_\theta(P(D))\le e^{-\gamma}\mu_\theta(D)$. Positive invariance permits iteration and gives \eqref{eq:disc-contract}. Finally, \eqref{eq:logjac} is affine in $\theta$, so the proof of Theorem~\ref{th:design} applies verbatim with $a(x)=\ln J_P(x)$ and $b(x)=\psi(P(x))-\psi(x)$.
head: environment

label: cor:discrete-invariant
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The sets $P^k(B)$ are nested and have finite $\mu_\theta$-measure. By \eqref{eq:disc-contract},
$\mu_\theta(P^k(B))\le e^{-k\gamma}\mu_\theta(B)\to0$. Continuity of finite measures from above gives $\mu_\theta(A_\infty)=0$, and \eqref{eq:equivmeas} gives the Riemannian null-measure statement. Moreover, $P(A_\infty)=A_\infty$: the inclusion $P(A_\infty)\subseteq A_\infty$ is immediate, while for $y\in A_\infty$ the unique $x\in B$ with $P(x)=y$ belongs to every $P^k(B)$ by injectivity of $P$, hence $x\in A_\infty$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Theorem~\ref{th:discrete} applies directly to a Poincar\'e return map on a transverse section whenever the return map is well defined and injective on the region of interest. It is intentionally stated as a discrete-time theorem rather than obtained by formally applying a continuous-time flow theorem to a map.
head: environment

label: th:distance
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Applying the Proposition \ref{prop:transport} to the smooth nonnegative weight $\delta_N\rho_\theta$ gives
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal M_{N,\theta}(\Phi_t(D))
=\int_{\Phi_t(D)}\rho_\theta
\big(\mathcal{L}_f\delta_N+\delta_ND_\theta f\big)dV_g.
\]
Condition \eqref{eq:moment-cond} and Gronwall's inequality yield \eqref{eq:moment-contract}. For an individual trajectory, \eqref{eq:pointwise-distance} gives
$\delta_N(\Phi_t(x))\le e^{-2\eta t}\delta_N(x)$; taking square roots gives \eqref{eq:distance-exp}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The two conclusions of Theorem~\ref{th:distance} are logically distinct. Condition \eqref{eq:moment-cond} controls an integral quantity for transported sets. Pointwise exponential attraction to $N$ follows only from the additional differential inequality \eqref{eq:pointwise-distance} (or another genuine pointwise stability argument).
head: environment

label: prop:conformal
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If a metric is multiplied by the scalar factor $\rho_\theta^{2/n}$, its determinant is multiplied by $\rho_\theta^2$, hence its volume form by $\rho_\theta$, proving \eqref{eq:vol-conformal}. The divergence with respect to a volume form $\rho_\theta dV_g$ is $\rho_\theta^{-1}\operatorname{div}_g(\rho_\theta f)$, which equals \eqref{eq:div-conformal} by Proposition~\ref{prop:transport}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For the scalar family $\rho_\alpha=w^\alpha$, the conformal metric is
$\widetilde g_\alpha=w^{2\alpha/n}g$. In particular, $\alpha=1$ gives $w^{2/n}g$, not $wg$ unless $n=2$.
head: environment
